d: Chinese, born 1957. Sculpture, installation, photography and editions.

x: Amanza Smith is an American artist from Indiana, known to television viewers from the property series Selling Sunset, who began painting during a long stay in hospital. Her mixed media canvases combine robotic figures, circuitry and graffiti-like marks.

d: Born Mexico City, 1991. Painter.
x: Ana Segovia was born in Mexico City in 1991 and works there. Segovia paints in oil, mostly figures taken from Mexican cowboy imagery and golden-age cinema, and has recently added video and charcoal drawing.

x: Andy Warhol was an American artist, born Andrew Warhola in Pittsburgh on 6 August 1928, who died in New York on 22 February 1987. x: Daniel Arsham is an American artist born in Cleveland in 1980 and raised in Miami, according to Highsnobiety and Ocula. d: British, born 1968. Drawings, prints, sculpture and animation.

x: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter, born in Coyoacán in 1907, who died in 1954, according to Wikipedia. Most of her paintings are small self-portraits. d: American, born 1950. Text works in posters, LED signs, stone and editions.
x: Jenny Holzer is an American artist born in Gallipolis, Ohio, in 1950, who has worked with words since the late 1970s, according to the Guggenheim in Venice. x: Keith Haring was born in Reading, Pennsylvania, on 4 May 1958 and died in New York on 16 February 1990, aged 31. Phillips Sotheby's

t: Gallery Activity in 2025: What Dealers Sold, and Who Bought
d: Galleries sold an estimated US$34.8 billion in 2025. Smaller dealers grew, mid-sized ones slipped, and almost half of all buyers were new to the gallery they bought from.
x: Gallery activity market-intelligence research Auctions publish their results lot by lot. Galleries mostly do not, so the clearest picture of what dealers sold comes once a year, in the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report. This piece sets out what the 2026 edition found about dealers in 2025, and what those figures can and cannot tell a collector. Where the figures come from The report is written by the economist Clare McAndrew of Arts Economics and published by Art Basel and UBS. Its dealer figures are built largely from surveys of dealers, so they are estimates, not counted sales. Art Basel also runs art fairs, which makes it an interested party in any figure about fairs. We have taken every figure below from Art Basel's own summaries of the report, which are listed at the end. The headline Dealers, which in the report means galleries and other private sellers, sold an estimated US$34.8 billion of art and antiques in 2025, up 2% on 2024. Art Basel calls this a return to stability after two years of decline. Public auction sales grew faster, up 9% to US$20.7 billion. The whole market came to an estimated US$59.6 billion. So galleries still sold more than auction houses by value, but their share of growth was smaller. How dealers of different sizes did The report groups dealers by turnover. Their results went in different directions. Dealers by yearly turnover Change in average sales, 2025 Under US$500,000 Up by double digits (exact figure not given in the summary) US$1 million to US$10 million Down 1% Over US$10 million Up 3%, after two years of decline Across all dealers, 42% reported higher sales than in 2024, 33% lower and 25% about the same. Costs rose too. Operating costs went up by about 5% on average, more than sales did, and 38% of dealers said they were less profitable. Who bought For collectors, the buyer figures are the most telling part of the report. New buyers. Of the people who bought from a dealer in 2025, 49% had not bought from that dealer before, up from 44% in 2024. At the smallest dealers, with turnover under US$250,000, the share was 60%. At the largest, over US$10 million, it was 39%. Fewer buyers each. The average dealer sold to 57 different buyers in the year, the lowest number since 2021. Dealers under US$250,000 sold to 29 on average, a fall of 40%. Closer to home. More than half of dealers said higher taxes, duties and paperwork had put off some international sales. At the smallest dealers, local collectors made up 71% of sales to private buyers, up 9%. At the largest, the local share was 29%, up 6%. Read together, these suggest smaller galleries were finding new buyers but selling to fewer people overall, and more of them nearby. That is our reading of the figures, not the report's. Where dealers sold Art fairs accounted for 35% of dealer sales in 2025, up 4% and the highest share since 2022. Most of that came at fairs abroad: 63% of fair sales were overseas and 37% at local fairs. Dealers with turnover of US$1 million to US$10 million leaned on fairs most, with their fair share rising from 29% to 36%. For the largest dealers it fell slightly, to 32%. Online-only sales across the whole market came to US$9.2 billion, 15% of the total and the lowest share since 2019. The summary does not give a separate online figure for dealers. What sold The report's summary says sales by dealers in Old Masters rose 9% and by dealers in modern art 11% by value, while contemporary art dealers were flat. Works by women made up 37% of dealer sales by value, up from 28% in 2018. At galleries working mainly on the primary market, selling new work for living artists, women were half of the artists represented. Openings and closures Gallery closures make headlines. The report reviewed galleries that announced a significant change in 2025. Of those changes, 42% were openings, 25% closures and 33% relocations or other changes. t: Zara Muse Auction Results: A Documented Market Timeline
d: Every public sale since her September 2024 debut at Tate Ward, with prices, houses and dates set side by side.
x: Auction results research auction-results Zara Muse has a short public auction record: six priced results in a little over two years, at three London houses. This is what the record shows, and where it runs out. The record so far Each row below keeps three figures apart: the estimate the house published before the sale, the hammer price, and the total the buyer paid once the buyer's premium was added. All six sales were in pounds. What the figures show The first result came on 18 September 2024, when In Her Own Light (2023) sold at Tate Ward for a hammer price of £27,000 against an estimate of £6,000 to £8,000. With premium the buyer paid £33,750. Three months later The Shape of Stillness (2024) made a hammer price of £38,000 at the same house, against £8,000 to £12,000, for a total of £47,500. The highest documented price is still the Bonhams sale of 3 April 2025. Malala Yousafzai, a portrait painted in 2019, sold for £51,200 with premium in the 20th/21st Century Art Day Sale at New Bond Street. Bonhams does not publish hammer prices, so we worked that one back from the total: about £40,000. The next result was lower. Alya (2023) closed at £33,280 with premium in a Bonhams online sale on 18 June 2026, against an estimate of £7,000 to £10,000. Our calculated hammer price is £26,000. Two paintings have since sold in online sales at Christie's in London, each against an estimate of £6,000 to £8,000. Ava (2025) made £44,450 with premium on 2 July 2026. Unspoken (2025) made £30,720 with premium on 21 October 2026. Christie's publishes the price realised, which includes the buyer's premium, and not the hammer price. We have now worked the hammer prices back from Christie's published rates: £35,000 for Ava, sold under the 27% rate, and £24,000 for Unspoken, sold after the rate rose to 28% on 1 September 2026. Both come out as round figures, which is a good sign the rates are right. Our guide to the buyer's premium shows the working. How to read it Three things stand out, and each needs a caution. Every priced lot beat its estimate by a wide margin. Hammer prices came in at roughly three times the high estimate at Tate Ward and about two and a half times at Bonhams in 2026. At Christie's our calculated hammer prices were about four and a half times and three times the high estimate. That tells you bidders went well past the guide. It also tells you the guides were set low compared with where bidding ended. The record has not risen in a straight line. In date order the totals run £33,750, £47,500, £51,200, £33,280, £44,450 and £30,720. These are six different paintings, of different sizes and subjects, sold in different kinds of sale. A lower result is not proof of a fall, and the earlier climb was not proof of a trend. The sample is small. Six priced results cannot tell you what a seventh painting will make. They show what six works made on six days. What we could not confirm The hammer prices for Ava and Unspoken are our calculation from Christie's published rates, not figures Christie's has stated. We also have not confirmed the estimate Bonhams published for Malala Yousafzai. A note on the 2025 record. Some reports give the Malala Yousafzai price in US dollars, at about $67,200. That is a conversion of the same £51,200 sale, not a separate result. We show every price in the currency of the sale. If you hold a catalogue, invoice or saleroom notice that fills one of these gaps, tell us and we will update the timeline and credit the source.

t: Konn Artiss Auction Results: Early Secondary-Market Activity
d: The first Tate Ward appearances, read against their estimates and the small sample they represent.
x: Auction results research auction-results Konn Artiss is better known for interventions than for objects. The name has been attached to a floating protest in Venice and to blocks of ice left outside Frieze London. Works have now started to appear at auction. Here is what has sold, and how much weight two results can carry. Who is selling what Konn Artiss works anonymously. The Art Newspaper has called it an "elusive art collective", while other reports describe a single street artist. For market purposes the distinction matters less than this: until 2026 there was no public resale record at all. The two documented results Untitled (2025) was lot 173 in Tate Ward's online sale with Artsy, By Collectors For Collectors, which closed on 14 May 2026. It carried an estimate of £6,000 to £8,000 and sold for £10,625 with premium. Tate Ward does not show hammer prices on its results pages, so we worked this one back from the total: about £8,500, a little above the high estimate. Gilded Promise (2025) was lot 160 at Tate Ward with the same £6,000 to £8,000 estimate. It sold for £15,000 with premium, which implies a hammer price of about £12,000, or one and a half times the high estimate. Tate Ward's lot page dates the sale to 24 June 2026, in its Urban & Contemporary Art auction. What two sales can tell you There is a bid. Both lots sold, and both sold above the top of their estimates. Somebody was willing to pay those sums in public. The works reached auction quickly. Both are dated 2025 and both were resold by 2026. Fast resale can mean demand. It can also mean an early owner chose to take a price. The results do not say which. Everything so far is at one house. A record built at a single saleroom is narrower than one tested at several, with different audiences and different specialists setting the estimates. What they cannot tell you Two results are not a market. They do not show how many bidders took part, who consigned the works, or what the same pieces would make if offered again. They say nothing about works that may have been offered privately or withdrawn. We will add each new sale to the Konn Artiss market profile as it is documented, including any lot that fails to sell. Unsold lots belong in the record too.

t: How an Art Auction Works, From Consignment to Collection
d: The steps every lot goes through, and what each one means for the price you later read.
x: Guide collecting-valuation market-intelligence research Every price on this site is the last step of a process that starts months before the sale. Knowing the steps makes the figures easier to read, and it shows where the gaps in a published result come from. 1. Consignment The owner, called the consignor, agrees to let an auction house offer the work. Between them they settle the estimate, the reserve and the seller's commission. The commission is agreed privately and is almost never published, which is one reason a hammer price does not tell you what the seller took home. Some sellers are also given a guarantee: a promise that the work will sell for at least an agreed sum, whatever happens in the room. How that works, and how to spot it, is covered in our guide to guarantees and catalogue symbols . 2. The catalogue and the estimate The house publishes an entry for each lot with a low and a high estimate. Phillips' guide for buyers in New York says a bid inside that range "should, in our opinion, offer a chance of success", and that estimates do not include the buyer's premium. An estimate is the house's opinion, and it is also a sales tool. It is not a valuation. The entry also gives the house's view of who made the work, its condition and its history. Sotheby's states that these are statements of opinion. Our guide to provenance, authentication and condition explains what sits behind them. 3. The reserve The reserve is the confidential lowest price the seller will accept. Phillips says its reserves are generally set at a percentage of the low estimate and never above it. The figure is not published, before the sale or after it. Below the reserve, the auctioneer can bid for the seller. Phillips' guide says the auctioneer may open the bidding on the seller's behalf and keep bidding for the seller up to the reserve. A commentary from the Center for Art Law describes these as bids taken "off the chandelier": bids from nobody in the room, used to keep things moving and to hide where the reserve sits. Someone watching a sale usually cannot tell which early bids are real. 4. Bidding There are four usual ways to bid: in the room with a numbered paddle, by telephone through a member of staff, online, or with an absentee bid left with the house beforehand. Phillips asks for absentee bids at least 24 hours before the sale, each with a maximum that leaves out the premium. Its staff then try to buy at the lowest price that the reserve and the other bidders allow. If two absentee bids match, the one received first wins. Bids go up in steps called increments. Phillips uses steps of up to about 10 per cent, at the auctioneer's discretion. 5. The hammer When bidding stops above the reserve, the auctioneer brings the hammer down. The winning bid is the hammer price. It is the figure the seller's proceeds are worked out from, and the figure the buyer's premium is charged on. 6. The premium and other charges The buyer then pays the buyer's premium on top of the hammer price, plus any tax. At Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips the standard rate on the first band of the hammer price is now 28 or 29 per cent. Our guide to the buyer's premium sets out the current rates and shows how to work a hammer price back from a published total. In the UK, a resale of work by a living artist, or by one who died less than 70 years ago, can also carry the Artist's Resale Right. This is a royalty on a sliding scale that starts at 4 per cent, and lots it applies to are marked in the catalogue. 7. If the lot does not sell If bidding stops short of the reserve, the lot is "bought in", also called passed. It goes back to the seller, or to the house if the house guaranteed it. Unsold lots often drop out of results lists and press reports. The Center for Art Law article cites a 2008 study which found that works that failed at auction later sold for about 30 per cent less. t: What Does an Auction Result Actually Tell Collectors?
d: One price, one room, one day. What a result records and what it leaves out.
x: Auction education market-intelligence collecting-valuation research An auction result is the most public number in the art market, which is why it gets quoted so often. It is also a narrow one. It records what happened to one object, in one sale, on one day. What a result does record A published result usually gives you four facts. The hammer price. The winning bid, called when the auctioneer's hammer falls. It is the figure the seller's proceeds are worked out from. The price with buyer's premium. The hammer price plus the fee the house charges the buyer. Most houses publish this total, and most headlines quote it. The estimate. The low and high guide the house printed before the sale. The basics of the sale. Date, house, sale title, lot number and currency. The gap between the first two is not small. On the two Zara Muse lots sold at Tate Ward in 2024, the published totals were exactly 25 per cent above the hammer prices. A reader comparing a hammer price from one source with a premium-inclusive price from another is comparing two different things. What it leaves out Who was bidding. A lot needs only two determined bidders to run far past its estimate. It can also sell to a single bidder at the reserve. The result looks the same either way. Who bought and who sold. Buyers and sellers are almost never named. Dealers, collectors and people with a stake in an artist's prices can all bid. Whether the price was arranged in advance. Some lots carry guarantees or irrevocable bids. Catalogues mark these with symbols, but summaries of results rarely repeat them. Condition, size and quality. A database line does not tell you that one painting is twice the size of another, or that one has been restored. What did not sell. Lots that fail to reach their reserve are "bought in". They often drop out of the story, though they say as much about demand as the sales do. Private prices. Gallery and private sales are not reported at all. Five questions to ask of any result Is this the hammer price or the price with premium? What was the estimate, and how did the house arrive at it? What currency was the sale in, and has someone converted it? How does this work compare in size, date and subject with the artist's other sold works? How many other results are there, and how many lots went unsold? None of this makes auction results useless. They are the best public evidence there is. They just need to be read as evidence of one sale, not as a price tag for an artist. Our auction results pages are laid out to make those five questions easy to answer. For the steps behind a result, read how an art auction works and the buyer's premium explained .

t: What Makes an Artist's Work Valued, and What a Price Cannot Tell You
d: Museums, prizes and scarcity shape prices. They do not settle whether a work is good. A sourced look at the artists we cover.

There are, though, a few things that buyers, museums and valuers look at again and again, and most of them can be checked. What tends to sit behind a price Recognition by museums. Solo shows at major museums, works in permanent collections and invitations to events such as the Venice Biennale. These reflect the judgement of curators, and they make an artist's work visible to more buyers. Prizes and honours. Awards such as the Praemium Imperiale or the Golden Lion at Venice mark a career as a whole. A place in art history. t: Why One Record Sale Does Not Establish Market Value
d: A record is a single data point. Value needs repeat sales, depth of bidding and time.
x: Collecting economics market-intelligence collecting-valuation research "New auction record" is the art market's favourite headline. It is true by definition and tells you very little. A record is the single highest price in a set of results. Market value is about what is likely, and the highest point in a set is the least likely place for the next result to land. A record is about one object Artists do not have prices. Works do. A record attaches to a particular painting: its size, its subject, its date and its condition. Take the highest documented price for Zara Muse, £51,200 with premium at Bonhams in April 2025. The work was a large portrait, 152 by 122 centimetres, of one of the most recognisable people in the world. The three priced results since then, all for different paintings in online sales during 2026, were £33,280, £44,450 and £30,720. None of these figures is "the value of a Zara Muse". Each is what one painting made. Two bidders are enough An auction price is set by the second most determined person in the room. If two people badly want the same lot, the price can end up far from where anyone else would have stopped. That is a real sale and a real price. It is not evidence that a third or fourth buyer exists at that level. Estimates can flatter a result Houses often set estimates low to draw in bidders. A lot that sells for four times a cautious estimate makes a better story than one that sells within a realistic one, even when the final prices are the same. Multiples of the estimate say as much about how the guide was set as about demand. What does establish value Valuers and experienced collectors look for a pattern, not a peak. Repeat sales. Many results for comparable works, ideally including the same work sold twice. Sell-through. The share of lots offered that find a buyer. A record sitting beside several unsold lots is a warning, not a comfort. Depth. Evidence of several bidders, at more than one house, in more than one city. Time. Prices that hold up across different years and different market moods. Agreement with the primary market. Auction results and gallery prices that sit in a sensible relation to each other. Why the word "value" needs care There is more than one kind. An insurance valuation is the cost of replacing a work at retail. Fair market value is what a willing buyer and seller would agree with no pressure on either. An auction estimate is a sales tool. A record sale is none of these. If you need a valuation for insurance, tax or a sale, ask a qualified valuer who has seen the work. We report records because they are facts. We try never to report them alone. On every artist market profile the highest price sits next to every other documented result, including the lower ones.

t: Unique Works, Prints and Editions: Why We Keep Them Apart
d: A canvas, a numbered print and a proof can carry the same name and sell for very different sums. How to tell them apart.
x: Guide collecting-valuation research Many of the artists on this site sell both unique works and editions. A search for an artist's name brings back both, side by side, and the gap between them can be very large. That is why our tables list unique works and name editions separately in the text. What an edition is Tate defines an edition as a set of identical copies made from a master, most often prints pulled from the same printing surface. Since the late 19th century most print runs have been limited and declared in advance. Each print is numbered: in an edition of 25, the prints are marked 1/25, 2/25 and so on. The bottom number is the size of the edition, and according to the International Fine Print Dealers Association it does not count the proofs. Editions are not only prints. Sculpture, photographs and video are editioned too. The KAWS COMPANION sold at Christie's in June 2026 was number 3 in an edition of three, with two artist's proofs. The letters you will see AP, artist's proof. Prints made in addition to the edition, kept by the artist. Tate notes that they are the same as the edition prints. PP, printer's proof. Copies given to the printer or publisher. HC, hors commerce. French for "not for sale". The IFPDA says these are often used as exhibition copies and may or may not differ from the edition. BAT, bon à tirer. "Good to print". The single proof the artist approves as the standard for the whole edition. Trial proof. A working proof made before the plate or screen is finished. Tate is clear that this is not the same thing as an artist's proof. Restrike. A later print not authorised by the artist or the artist's heirs. Signed, or signed in the plate The IFPDA says a print described simply as "signed" should be signed by hand in pencil, ink or crayon. A signature printed as part of the image is "signed in the plate", which is a different thing. It also draws a line between an original digital print, which the artist made as a print, and a digital copy of a work in another medium, which is a reproduction. t: Guarantees, Irrevocable Bids and the Symbols in a Catalogue
d: Some lots are sold before the sale starts. The small symbols next to a lot number tell you which.
x: Guide collecting-valuation market-intelligence research Some lots arrive at auction already backed by a promise made before the sale. That promise changes what the final price tells you, so it is worth knowing how to spot it. The house guarantee With a house guarantee, the auction house promises the seller a minimum price whatever happens in the room. If the lot sells for less, the house makes up the difference. If it does not sell, the house pays the guaranteed sum and owns the work. The seller gets certainty, and the house wins a consignment it might otherwise have lost to a rival. The third party guarantee, or irrevocable bid A house can pass that risk to someone else. Before the sale, a third party commits to buy the lot at an agreed figure, usually through a written bid that cannot be withdrawn. Boodle Hatfield, a London law firm, describes this as an irrevocable written bid placed for a fee, for an amount that is not disclosed. If no one bids higher, the third party buys the work. If someone does, the third party is paid a fee, or a share of the price above the guarantee. Phillips' guide for buyers says the fee can be fixed or a percentage of the hammer price. Christie's notes that a third party who wins the lot still pays the full hammer price and premium. Boodle Hatfield points out that the fee can work as a discount, so the price published for the lot may not be what the guarantor paid in the end. It also says guarantees tend to sit close to the low estimate. How to spot them Catalogues mark these lots with symbols, explained in a key printed with the conditions of sale. Phillips, for example, uses: ○ for a lot Phillips has guaranteed itself. ♦ for a lot with a third party guarantee. Δ for a lot Phillips owns in whole or in part. • for a lot offered with no reserve. Other houses use their own symbols, so check the key in the catalogue you are reading. The auctioneer may also announce at the start of a sale that some lots are guaranteed. The amount of a guarantee is never published. Why it matters when you read a result The lot was always going to find an owner. If nobody bids, the house or the guarantor takes it, so a sale is not by itself proof of open demand. One bid may be the whole story. If the guarantor is the only bidder, the result shows one party's pre-agreed price. The guarantor knows more than you. Boodle Hatfield notes concerns that guarantors are often a house's biggest clients, and that they know the guaranteed figure when the room does not. None of this makes a guaranteed result false. It is a real sale at a real price. It is one more thing to ask about before reading much into it. What our tables show Our tables do not yet record whether a lot was guaranteed, because most results pages do not repeat the catalogue symbols. Where we can see a symbol on the lot page, we will add it to the notes for that artist. Sources Boodle Hatfield, Auction house guarantees: friend or foe? t: Provenance, Authentication and Condition: What Sits Behind a Price
d: Two works that look alike can sell far apart. Often the reason is in the paperwork, not the picture.
x: Guide collecting-valuation research An auction price is paid for more than an image. It is paid for a particular object with a particular history, and for the confidence a buyer has in who made it and what state it is in. Those three things, provenance, authentication and condition, explain many of the gaps between results. Provenance Provenance is a work's ownership history, from the studio to today. A clear record helps in two ways. It supports the attribution, and it shows that the work can be sold legally. A gap, especially in periods of war or upheaval, can make buyers wary. A distinguished owner, a museum loan or a well known exhibition in the record can add interest. History can even change what a work is. In 2018 a Banksy painting, Girl with Balloon, shredded itself just after the hammer fell at a Sotheby's sale. Renamed Love is in the Bin, it was offered again at Sotheby's London on 14 October 2021. The Art Newspaper reported a hammer price of £16m and £18.6m with fees, against £1m at the 2018 sale. What the catalogue wording means Auction catalogues use set phrases to show how sure the house is. Sotheby's explains that the artist's name on its own means that, in its opinion, the work is by the artist. "Attributed to" means it is probably by the artist, with less certainty. Sotheby's also says that any statement about authorship, date, provenance or condition is a statement of opinion. The exact wording matters, and two lots with the same name at the top can be described with different confidence. Authentication: the Banksy example Some artists, estates or foundations run their own authentication. Banksy's is the clearest case among the artists on this site. His office, Pest Control, says it is the only body authorised to authenticate his work and issues certificates of authenticity. Its published terms say: Work made in a public space, or removed from one, is not eligible. Street pieces are not authenticated. Checking a screenprint costs £100 plus VAT, and an original £150 plus VAT. There is no charge if the work is found to be fake. Pest Control decides at its own discretion and does not have to give reasons. A buyer can ask it to check a work before buying, but only if the work already has a Pest Control certificate. New owners can register a change of ownership. Condition Damage, repair, fading and old varnish all affect what a buyer will pay. Houses will usually provide a condition report on request. Phillips says its staff who write them are not professional restorers or conservators, and encourages buyers to inspect the work or bring their own adviser. A condition report is a starting point, not a guarantee. Reading results with this in mind A database line rarely mentions provenance or condition. When two results for similar works are far apart, look at the lot pages. The difference is often there: a better history, a cleaner surface, or a firmer attribution. t: Understanding Liquidity in Emerging Contemporary Art
d: How often work changes hands, how quickly, and why that matters more than the top price.
x: Artist-market research market-intelligence research Liquidity is a simple idea with an awkward name. It means how easily you can turn something back into money, at a price close to what you expected, when you choose to. Shares in a large company are very liquid. A painting by an artist with a handful of auction results is not. Why price is the wrong first question Most writing about emerging artists is about how high prices have gone. For anyone who might one day sell, the better questions are whether there will be a buyer, how long a sale will take and how much of the price will be lost along the way. An artist can have a striking record and almost no liquidity. How to judge it There is no single measure, but five signs are worth checking. How many works come up each year. A handful of lots a year is a thin market. Dozens is a deeper one. How many of them sell. The sell-through rate. Results pages often leave out unsold lots, so look for a source that lists them. Where they sell. One house or several. One city or several. How results sit against estimates. Results scattered far above and below the guide suggest nobody is sure of the level. How long the record is. A market that has only existed in good times has not been tested. By these measures the two emerging artists we track are at an early stage. Zara Muse has six priced results over 25 months at three houses. Konn Artiss has two, at one. That is a description, not a criticism. Every auction record starts somewhere. The contrast with an established market is plain on this site: Gerhard Richter and Yayoi Kusama each have at least five documented lots from 2026 alone, offered in three cities, and those are only the most recent we list. The cost of getting in and out Art is expensive to trade, and the costs fall on both sides. The buyer pays the hammer price plus a buyer's premium. The seller receives the hammer price less a seller's commission and any agreed costs such as photography, insurance and shipping. In the UK the Artist's Resale Right can add a royalty for living artists on qualifying sales. A worked example. In September 2024 a Zara Muse painting sold at Tate Ward for a hammer price of £27,000. The buyer paid £33,750 with premium. Seller's commission is negotiated and not published. If it had been 10 per cent, the seller would have received £24,300 before other costs. On that assumption about 28 per cent of what the buyer paid, £9,450, did not reach the seller. So a buyer who resold the same work at the same hammer price would be well short of getting their money back. Why thin markets move sharply When only a few works are offered each year, one or two keen bidders can lift prices quickly, and their absence can drop them just as fast. Supply matters as well. In a young market much of the work is still with the artist, the gallery and first buyers. If several owners decide to sell in the same season, there may not be enough bidders to go round. What this means in practice Buy work because you want to live with it, and treat any resale value as uncertain. If resale matters to you, look at the breadth of the record before the height of it. And remember that selling takes time: consigning, cataloguing and waiting for the right sale can take months. Nothing here is investment advice. It is a way of reading the record with clear eyes.

t: How to Compare Primary Gallery Prices with Auction Results
d: Gallery prices and auction prices measure different things. A method for reading them together.
x: Collecting economics collecting-valuation research Collectors are often shown an auction result as proof that a gallery price is fair, or a bargain. The two numbers can be compared, but only with care, because they come from markets that work in different ways. Two markets, two kinds of price The primary market is the first sale of a work, usually through the artist's gallery. The price is set in advance, tends to follow the size of the work, and moves slowly. Galleries generally raise prices in steps and avoid cutting them. The secondary market is every sale after that, including auctions. Auction prices are set by whoever turns up to bid. They can jump or fall from one sale to the next. A gallery price is an asking price that someone has agreed to. An auction price is the result of a contest. One is steady by design. The other is not. A method in six steps Match the work. Compare paintings with paintings and prints with prints. Match size, year and series as closely as you can. A unique canvas and an edition of fifty are different goods. Use the right auction figure. If you are asking "what would I pay?", use the price with buyer's premium. If you are asking "what would I get if I sold?", start from the hammer price and take off a seller's commission. Put both in the same currency and on the same tax basis. Check whether the gallery price includes VAT and whether a converted auction price used the rate on the day of the sale. Look at all the results. Use every comparable sale, including the low ones and any unsold lots, not only the best. Check the dates. A result from two years ago and a price list from this month are not describing the same moment. Write down what you do not know. Who bid, who consigned, whether the lot was guaranteed, and what condition it was in. Reading the gap When auction results sit above gallery prices, it can mean demand is running ahead of supply. It does not mean you could buy at the gallery and sell at that auction price. You would receive the hammer price less commission, on a different day, with different bidders, for a different work. When auction results sit below gallery prices, it does not prove the gallery is overcharging. Galleries sell with services attached: choice of work, provenance from the studio, and a relationship. It does tell you that resale may not return what you paid. When there are only a few results, the honest reading is that the comparison is not yet reliable. A caution about interested parties Galleries, artists and existing collectors all benefit when an artist's auction prices are strong, and any of them may bid. That is a normal feature of the art market, and it is one reason a result cannot be read as a neutral measure of outside demand. It applies to the artists covered on this site as much as to any other. Our own position is set out on the about page . The short version Compare like with like, use the right figure for the question you are asking, and treat a small number of results as a small amount of evidence. For anything that turns on a specific figure, such as insurance or a sale, speak to a qualified valuer.

d: The winning bid, called when the auctioneer's hammer falls. It does not include fees. The seller's proceeds are worked out from it.
The fee an auction house charges the buyer on top of the hammer price. It is a percentage that varies by house and by price band.
The hammer price plus the buyer's premium. This is the figure most houses publish and most headlines quote. Also called the price realised.
The low and high guide a house prints before the sale. It is a sales tool as well as a forecast, and is often set to attract bidding.
The confidential minimum the seller will accept. By convention it is not set above the low estimate.
A lot that fails to reach its reserve and goes unsold. Also called passed.
The share of lots offered that sell. A basic measure of demand for an artist or a sale.
Handing a work to an auction house or dealer to sell on your behalf. The terms are set out in a consignment agreement.
The fee the house takes from the seller, deducted from the hammer price. It is negotiable and rarely published.

A royalty due to living artists, and to their estates for 70 years, when a work is resold through the trade above a set threshold. In the UK it is charged on a sliding scale that starts at 4 per cent. Lots it applies to are usually marked ARR.
The first sale of a work, usually by the artist's gallery at a set price.
Any later sale of a work, including auctions and private resales.
How easily a work can be sold, at a price near expectations, at a time of the owner's choosing.
A promise by the house or a third party that a lot will sell for at least an agreed sum. Guaranteed lots are marked in the catalogue.
The ownership history of a work, from the studio to the present.
The price a willing buyer and a willing seller would agree, with neither under pressure and both properly informed. It is not the same as an insurance value or an auction record.
One work, or a group of works, offered under a single number in an auction.
The numbered card a registered bidder raises to bid in the saleroom.
A written maximum bid left with the house before the sale. Staff bid for you up to that figure, as cheaply as the other bids allow. Also called a commission bid.
The step by which bids rise, set by the auctioneer. Phillips works in steps of up to about 10 per cent.
Bids the auctioneer takes on the seller's behalf, below the reserve, to open or keep the bidding going. They do not come from a buyer.
A written bid placed before the sale that cannot be withdrawn, usually by a third party in return for a fee. If nobody bids higher, that party buys the lot. It works as a guarantee.
A Phillips scheme. A binding written bid at or above the low estimate, left at least 48 hours before a live sale, is charged a lower buyer's premium.
Christie's name for the published price. It includes the buyer's premium.
A single original, such as a painting or drawing, as opposed to one copy from an edition.
A set of identical copies made from one master, such as prints from one plate or screen. Each copy is numbered, for example 12/50.
A print made in addition to the numbered edition and kept by the artist. It matches the edition prints.
A copy of the finished print given to the printer or publisher, outside the numbered edition.
French for "not for sale". Copies kept outside the edition, often for exhibitions.
A later print made without the authority of the artist or the artist's heirs.
Catalogue wording meaning the house thinks the work is probably by the artist, with less certainty than the artist's name alone.
A house's written note of a work's state: damage, repairs, fading. Useful, but not a guarantee, and not written by a conservator unless it says so.
A document from an artist, estate or approved body confirming a work is genuine. For Banksy, Pest Control is the body that issues them.
